1.pericope_label: Observe the month of Abib, and keep the passover unto the LORD thy God

schools.summary: Gill explains the name before the command: Abib, sometimes called Nisan, answered to part of March and part of April and took its name from the corn then appearing in the ear, when all things were in their verdure — the Greek translators simply calling it the month of new fruit. It was appointed first of the months for sacred purposes, and was the month of the exodus and of the first passover. Calvin looks past the mechanics to the purpose, having already treated the institution under the First Commandment, since the Passover was a symbol of redemption in which the people exercised themselves in the pure worship of the one God, acknowledging him as their only Father and distinguishing him from every idol; and he presses what follows from the single sanctuary — one altar was prescribed, as if God would gather them under one banner for the preservation of concord and the unity of the faith.

Henry draws out the force of a command to observe the whole month when only one week of it was festival: their preparation beforehand, and their reflection upon it and improvement of it afterwards, were to be so serious as to amount to an observance of the month entire. He notes that the year had previously been reckoned to begin in September, and reports that the Chaldee paraphrasts would not read the deliverance as a departure by night, since there was an express order that no one should stir out of doors till morning — they therefore render the clause as meaning Israel came out by daylight, one expanding it as 'he brought thee out of Egypt, and did wonders by night', the other as 'and thou shalt eat the passover by night'. Henry also observes that the passover was itself a sacrifice, which is why Christ our passover is said to be sacrificed for us, and that no sacrifice was accepted except from the altar that sanctified it.

Wesley takes the night straightforwardly, against the Chaldee: it was in the night that Pharaoh was forced to give them leave to depart, so they made their preparations then and perfected the work in the morning; and he notes the change of the year's beginning was by a special order from God in remembrance of the deliverance. Clarke supplies the reason for the feast's name from the same night — the destroying angel, seeing the blood of the appointed sacrifice sprinkled on the lintels and door-posts of the Israelites' houses, passed over them and did not destroy any of their firstborn.

Keil and Delitzsch call it simply the earing month and observe that the precise day is not fixed here because it was already known from Exodus. They warn that the phrase rendered 'keep the passover' is being stretched: it is used primarily of preparing the paschal lamb for a festal meal, but is employed here in a wider sense, so that 'passover' covers not the lamb only but the paschal sacrifices generally — what the rabbins gather under the common name chagiga — meaning all the sacrifices slain during the seven days of unleavened bread, though not the burnt-offerings and sin-offerings prescribed elsewhere for the feast.

2.pericope_label: Sacrifice the passover in the place the LORD shall choose; seven days of unleavened bread

schools.summary: Gill fixes the time from the tradition — the fourteenth of Abib at night, between the two evenings, as the Targum of Jonathan has it — and takes the lamb as a type of Christ, the passover sacrificed for us. He glosses 'within any of thy gates' as the cities, so named because they commonly had gates in which public business was transacted, and understands the place where God would set his name of the ark and the mercy seat with the cherubim over them, meaning Jerusalem once Solomon had built the temple. On the command to roast he concedes that the Hebrew word properly signifies to boil, and that Onkelos so renders it, yet boiling the paschal lamb is expressly forbidden; some therefore refer the verse to the chagigah, and in Josiah's day the passover was roasted with fire while the other offerings were boiled in pots and pans — but the connection with the preceding verses persuades Gill it means the lamb, and he follows Jarchi in taking the word of roasting with fire despite its form. Calvin takes the bread of affliction of the escape rather than the bondage: by this sign they were reminded of getting away in haste, as it were out of the very flames, for they must have been in the greatest extremity when there was no time even to bake bread — so the loaf is so called in order that the manner of the deliverance may the more enhance God's grace.

Wesley resolves the difficulty of a passover taken from the flock and the herd, when the paschal victim was a lamb or kid only, by widening the noun: the word stands for the feast as a whole, so the clause may be rendered 'thou shalt observe the feast of the passover with sheep and with oxen', as the sacrifices appointed for those days require. He gives three reasons why the killing was confined to the sanctuary — that so great a work might be done with the solemnity God required; that this was a sacrifice and not a sacrament only, with the sprinkling of blood that is the essential part of one; and that it might mark out the place where Christ, the true passover, was to be slain. On the bread he will have both afflictions at once, bread neither usual nor pleasant, to remind them of the miseries endured in Egypt and of the hurry of coming out. Clarke takes it of the bondage alone: baked without leaven it was unsavoury, and its very taste put them in mind of their afflictive servitude.

9.pericope_label: Seven weeks shalt thou number: the feast of weeks, and rejoicing before the LORD

schools.summary: Gill sets out the reckoning — seven weeks numbered, then a second feast, called from the counting the feast of weeks and sometimes Pentecost from its being the fiftieth day — and notes that it was at this same feast, long afterwards, that the Spirit was poured out upon the apostles. Calvin fits it to the agricultural year, the Passover having fallen when the harvests were just beginning to ripen, and marks a coincidence he thinks worth noting: exactly this number of days lay between the departure from Egypt and the publication of the Law. He treats the command to rejoice as an argument rather than a mood. God exhorts them to willingness on the ground that his service brings this rejoicing with it, and nothing ought to stimulate obedience more than knowing that God consults our good rather than seeking advantage from us. Ungodly men rejoice too, wantonly and intemperately, but their laughter is turned into weeping and gnashing of teeth; so Moses magnifies this other joy as a peculiar blessing — to rejoice before God, as if a father should invite his children to delight themselves together with him. Since tranquillity of conscience, which alone brings true rejoicing, is wanting to the wicked, they do not actually enjoy the merriment they plunge into. Gill draws the practical conclusion from the closing charge to remember the bondage: it should make them liberal in the freewill offering, generous in the feast, and compassionate toward the stranger, the widow and the fatherless.

Clarke describes what such rejoicing looked like — the offerings eaten with festivity, shared with friends liberally and bestowed on the poor with great generosity, so that these too might partake with joy before the Lord — and then accounts for a related rule in a strikingly plain way: the flesh had to be eaten fresh, since in that climate putrefaction soon set in, which is why nothing was to remain until morning. That consideration, he says, is sufficient by itself, without recourse to the moral and evangelical reasons the learned and devout Ainsworth assigned; and he borrows Harmer's exclamation at how beneficent and cheerful the design of the whole institution is. Wesley notes only that the tribute asked was over and besides what had already been appointed.

13.pericope_label: Thou shalt observe the feast of tabernacles seven days, and thou shalt surely rejoice

schools.summary: Gill dates the feast to the fifteenth of Tisri, answering to September. Calvin explains why that month was chosen, and the reasoning is economic as much as liturgical: the first day was called the day of In-gathering because by then the produce of the whole year had been stored in the granaries and provision cellars, and since the people were resting from their rural labours it was a convenient season — so arranged by God precisely that they might go up to Jerusalem more willingly, the journey costing them little expense and little sacrifice of their domestic interests. He then finds a promise hidden inside what reads as a command. Where our version has 'when the LORD shall have blessed thee', the Hebrew stands literally as 'because he shall bless thee', and Moses is assuring them that if they devote their minds diligently to God's service they will never want grounds for rejoicing, since he will never interrupt the flow of his blessing; so the close of the verse is not a mere command but also a promise. Calvin weighs the small particle carefully, allowing that it may mean 'nevertheless' but noting it equally bears 'however', 'at any rate', or 'truly', and renders it 'only joyful, and not sad' — no sorrow or anxiety being admitted that might hinder the gladness the day required. Gill adds that the Targum of Jonathan brings in the flute and the pipe, instrumental music being used to increase the joy.

Keil and Delitzsch draw out who the rejoicing includes. The law simply enforces the observance of the feast at the central sanctuary and exhorts the people to rejoice at it — but the exhortation is not left to the household head and his own children: he is to allow not only his sons and daughters a share in that joy but the manservant and the maidservant too, together with the portionless Levites and the strangers among them.

16.pericope_label: Three times in a year shall all thy males appear before the LORD, and not empty

schools.summary: Gill asks why a requirement already given should be repeated, and his answer explains the shape of the whole chapter: it is set down again for the sake of naming the place at which they were to appear, which the earlier statements had not specified — indeed it is chiefly for that reason that the other festivals have been recited here at all. On the size of the gift he observes that the law fixes no quantity; the wise men appointed one afterwards, but the Lord left it to the generosity of the people, laying down only the rule that each give according to his ability and as God had prospered him, Jarchi putting it concretely that the man who has many eatables and much goods shall bring many burnt offerings and many peace offerings. Calvin asks who was actually bound, and answers with a series of concessions to human weakness: God would make allowance for the infirmity of his people and so did not impose five journeys a year, and required only the males to leave their houses — sparing the women, travelling being less convenient for them and, through the fruitfulness God had promised, they were almost always either pregnant or nursing. He reckons boys under twenty excepted too, since 'males' takes in only those comprised in the census. To the objection that in spiritual worship there is no difference between male and female, Calvin replies that the fathers of families presented themselves in the names of their wives and children, so the profession made there extended to the other sex and to those of tender age; and he hears David alluding to it in the psalm of a people who come with voluntary offerings in the day of thy assembly. A second objection he finds anticipated in the law itself: lest they should protest that stripping the land of its defenders invited invasion, God had promised that no one should so much as desire to assail their forsaken homes.

Keil and Delitzsch describe the repetition the same way Gill does — the law that the men appear three times a year at the three feasts just mentioned, now carrying the additional clause 'at the place which the LORD shall choose', together with an explanation of what it means not to appear empty, namely that every man is to bring according to his gift. Ellicott adds a detail from the parallel passage which does not appear here: a promise attached that their land should be safe while they were away from it.

18.pericope_label: Judges and officers shalt thou make thee in all thy gates: that which is altogether just shalt thou follow

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch put the second office higher than the others do: the word means literally writers, and these men were not merely messengers and servants of the courts but secretaries and advisers of the judges, named from their duty of keeping the genealogical lists, and already existing in Egypt. On appointment they hold that the nation is addressed as a whole and directed to appoint judges for itself — to choose them and have them inducted by its rulers, as at Sinai, where the people chose and Moses installed — and they add the sharp caution that election by majorities was unknown to the Mosaic law. Ellicott notes that a fresh synagogue section opens with these words, the land now being considered as the seat of the Kingdom of Jehovah, and points to Joshua as showing that such magistrates were already appointed.

Gill, following Maimonides, places the judges in the court of judicature and describes the officers as masters of the staff and the whip, who go out into the markets and streets and shops to regulate weights and measures and to smite all who do wrong, everything they do being by order of the judges; he renders the doubled word strictly as justice, justice, and nothing else. Calvin grants that popular election was a real privilege but denies it is a universal rule — it is not conceded to all peoples to elect their judges, God having honoured his chosen people with that prerogative, and what the passage recommends generally is regular government rather than any one method. Whether magistrates come by the suffrages of the people or are imposed in some other way, they are the necessary ministers of God to confine all men under the yoke of the laws, for public utility is what makes their authority agreeable, which it would otherwise be hateful. On the emphatic repetition Calvin explains that it inculcates the study of equity with inflexible constancy, and not without cause, since nothing is more likely than that men's minds should be clouded by favour or hatred, and there are so many quibbles by which justice is perverted that unless judges watch cautiously against deception they will often find themselves ensnared.

Henry leaves the method of appointment open — however the persons were pitched upon, whether by their sovereign's appointment or the people's election, the power was ordained of God — and counts it a great mercy that justice was brought to the people's doors, more expeditious and less expensive for them. He states the standard bluntly: better not judge at all than not judge with just judgment; and he turns the closing command into a series of demands, to adhere to the principles of justice, act by its rules, countenance its demands, imitate its patterns, and pursue with resolution whatever appears to be just.

Clarke reaches for English equivalents, the first office being much what our magistrates or justices of the peace are and the second like our inquest sergeants and beadles, who entered houses and shops to examine weights and measures and the conduct of the people and brought an offender before the magistrate to be punished on the spot; he notes they seem also to have served as heralds in the army, and observes that in China all minor offences are still punished on the spot in the magistrate's presence. Wesley describes the officers as subordinates who brought causes before the judge, made his sentence known and carried it out, and explains why the bribe is singled out: a gift biasses the mind so that a man cannot discern between right and wrong, and it works even on judges accustomed to righteous dealing. Wesley and Henry agree on the later shape of the system, a court of twenty-three judges in every town of more than a hundred and twenty families and a court of three in the smaller ones.

21.pericope_label: Thou shalt not plant thee a grove, neither set thee up any image, which the LORD hateth

schools.summary: Gill is careful to say what is not forbidden: the prohibition covers trees of any sort, but it was never unlawful to plant trees or even groves of them — only to plant them for a religious or idolatrous use. On the second prohibition he defines the term as a statue or pillar set up for idolatry, and reports Aben Ezra's important qualification, that what was not set up for idolatry was not forbidden at all, as when a stone was erected in memory of some action or remarkable event. Calvin sets the grove in the wider religious world and treats the rule as one of separation: among the heathen nations groves were sacred, so that no religious object could receive due reverence except under the shade of trees, and lest conformity with so general a custom should vitiate the pure worship of God this distinction was drawn — the intent being that the Jews should fly from all strange rites, in case by approaching the Gentiles too closely they should introduce a sinful medley. That it was needed appears from how eagerly they imitated the nations anyway, there being scarcely any period in which they abstained from the high places, and Isaiah and Jeremiah reproaching them for playing the harlot under every green tree. Calvin then faces a real contradiction: God elsewhere commands that stones be erected on the borders of the land with the sum of the Law inscribed on them, which would collide with this prohibition unless the statue meant here is a false image of God in which men set him before themselves in bodily form. He makes a small grammatical choice with a large result, referring the relative not to the image set up but to the act of setting it up, so that what is declared abominable is the erecting itself — for by that act God's glory is dishonoured, when he is transfigured into a body or anything corporeal is mixed with his spiritual nature.

Wesley gives the reason in a line: this was the practice of idolaters and might be an occasion of reviving idolatry. Clarke turns instead on visibility, observing that groves were planted about the idol temples for the sake of the obscene worship performed in them, and that God would therefore have no groves or thickets about his own altar, so that there might be no room even for the suspicion that anything contrary to the strictest purity was transacted there — every part of the divine worship being publicly performed, for the purpose of general edification.

Ellicott reaches Clarke's conclusion independently and in a sentence: the worship of Jehovah allowed of no secret rites, and nothing that might lead toward the abominations of heathen idolatry could be permitted near the altar. He adds that the Hebrew word is sometimes used of images but is here evidently used of the grove itself, and passes on Rashi's explanation of the second term as a single stone, whether statue or pillar. Keil and Delitzsch identify it more narrowly still as a memorial stone or stone pillar dedicated to Baal.
